notes: CCRC judicial review; Lord Bingham and Lord Woolf dismiss bad-faith challenge to non-referral in European Leisure fraud case.

enrichment.short_title: Ward v CCRC: judicial review of non-referral in European Leisure fraud convictions
key_facts: Mr Ward and Mr Howarth were convicted in 1995 of conspiracy to defraud and theft arising from a false market in European Leisure shares during the Midsummer Leisure bid.
They applied to the Criminal Cases Review Commission in 2000 after failed appeals; the Commission declined referral in September 2004 following a lengthy forensic investigation.
The claimants alleged bad faith, alleging Commission staff had encouraged them before reversing course and covering up misconduct by the SFO, DTI and police.

They sought permission to challenge the Commission's decision by judicial review on grounds including flawed OASys-style risk reasoning, Quadrini credibility and Inland Revenue material on Dantice invoices.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review following refusal by the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the court held the Commission's decision was reasonable and lawful and that unfounded allegations of bad faith against commissioners and caseworkers failed.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 29-style reference the CCRC's real-possibility judgment is entrusted to the Commission and the court on judicial review ensures only lawfulness, not merits substitution; encouraging comments by investigating staff do not bind the decision-making committee or vitiate a reasoned refusal to refer.
legal_issues: Whether the CCRC acted unlawfully or in bad faith in declining to refer the convictions
Whether comments by Mr Henderson and Mr Weiss created legitimate expectations binding the Commission
Whether new material on Quadrini, Dantice invoices and non-disclosure crossed the real-possibility threshold
The proper scope of judicial review of CCRC decisions under R v CCRC ex parte Pearson
linked_authorities: R v CCRC ex parte Pearson [1999] 3 All ER 498
R v CCRC ex parte Hunt [2001] 2 Cr.App. R. 71

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, CCRC role and final dismissal are comprehensively reasoned by the court.

notes: Lord Woolf CJ on CFA success fee reasonableness at inception and refusal of indemnity costs after liability settlement.

enrichment.short_title: Burton v Kingsley: CFA uplift and indemnity costs after RTA settlement
key_facts: Passengers Burton and Haynes were seriously injured when a car driven by Kingsbury left the A27; Harper, driving nearby, was also sued.
Liability was settled on the day of trial with judgment against Kingsbury and dismissal against Harper; the court then decided CFA uplift and costs basis issues.
CFAs dated 9 September 2001 provided a 100% success fee; the defendant contended 10–20% was reasonable.
Claimants' solicitors wrote on 30 April 2003 inviting admission of liability and threatening indemnity costs if none was forthcoming within 21 days.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Written decision on outstanding costs issues after settlement of liability on the day of the scheduled trial.
enrichment.outcome: Allowable CFA uplift fixed at 50%; claimants' liability costs ordered on the standard basis only; costs of the two issues treated as part of overall liability costs.
enrichment.ratio: The reasonableness of a pre-October 2003 CFA success fee is judged at the date the agreement was entered into, not at trial; a 100% uplift was excessive where prospects were strong but materially uncertain, and refusal of a Part 36-style letter did not justify indemnity costs where each defendant reasonably contested individual liability.
legal_issues: What uplift under old-regime CFAs was reasonable for passenger RTA claims with conflicting witness evidence
Whether the letter of 30 April 2003 justified indemnity costs under CPR 44.3
Application of Callery v Gray, Atack v Lee and KU v Liverpool City Council to a non-modest multi-defendant case
Costs of the CFA and indemnity issues themselves
linked_authorities: Callery v Gray (No.1) [2001] EWCA Civ 1117
Atack v Lee [2004] EWCA Civ 1712
KU v Liverpool City Council [2005] EWCA Civ 475

confidence.notes: CFA uplift figure and costs basis ruling are explicit though quantum remains for assessment.

notes: Wilkie J imposed general civil restraint order on vexatious litigant and permanently stayed three Claims Direct-related actions.

enrichment.short_title: Carroll v Kynaston: general civil restraint order after extended CRO breaches
key_facts: Peter Carroll and Christine Kynaston were embroiled in long-running litigation arising from their association with Claims Direct.
Carroll had been subject to an extended civil restraint order since 20 November 2003 but repeatedly breached its permission and notice procedures.
Kynaston applied for a general civil restraint order, permanent stay of three actions, and summary assessed costs.
Carroll also sought to commence proceedings against third parties including Ian Lee and Kynaston's former solicitors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for general civil restraint order, permanent stay and costs following breaches of an extended civil restraint order.
enrichment.outcome: Permanent stay ordered by consent on three actions; general civil restraint order imposed for two years; summary assessed costs of £600 awarded to Kynaston.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant persists in meritless applications and breaches an extended civil restraint order, including by threatening litigation against third parties outside its clear terms, a general civil restraint order is justified as the next step in the court's graduated control of vexatious conduct.
legal_issues: Whether Carroll breached the extended civil restraint order procedure
Whether a general civil restraint order was warranted under CPR Part 3.11 and PD 3C
Whether third-party defamation threats fell within the extended order
Appropriate permanent stay and costs where both parties wished litigation to end
linked_authorities: Bahamjee v Forsdick [2003] EWCA Civ 1113
Ashok Mahajan v Department of Constitutional Affairs [2004] EWCA Civ 946

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on individual breaches and final orders are clearly recorded.

notes: Peter Smith J dismissed liquidators' debt and undervalue claims; MCI payments treated as Mercury debt reductions.

enrichment.short_title: Stone & Rolls v MCI: insolvency claims over inter-company payments
key_facts: Liquidators of Stone & Rolls Ltd sued Micro Communications Inc for $928,272 plus interest on seven payments totalling about $2.9m made between 2000 and 2002.
SR had been found liable in the Commercial Court for a massive grain fraud orchestrated by Zvonko Stojevic, who controlled SR, Mercury Consultants and related companies.
MCI contended the payments reduced SR's admitted debt to Mercury and funded acquisition of the Vienna property and Bank of Austria debt.
The liquidators pursued both a loan claim and an undervalue claim under section 238 against a connected person.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of debt and transactions-at-an-undervalue claims by liquidators against MCI.
enrichment.outcome: Both the debt claim and the undervalue claim dismissed; payments were properly attributable to partial discharge of Mercury's debt rather than gifts or loans to MCI.
enrichment.ratio: Where contemporaneous banking instructions and ZS's fax of 5 March 2001 showed payments to MCI were made on Mercury's instruction in reduction of SR's subordinated debt and were used to acquire assets for the Stojevic group, liquidators could not infer an unsecured loan or undervalue gift on the balance of probabilities.
legal_issues: Whether T1–T7 were loans to MCI or debt reductions benefiting SR via Mercury
Construction of Fortis Bank subordination and acknowledgement of debt agreements
Whether SR and MCI were connected persons through ZS's control
Admissibility and weight of documentation created by a dishonest controller
linked_authorities: Komercni Banka v Stone & Rolls [2003] 1 Lloyd's Rep 383
Rhesa Shipping Co SA v Edmunds [1985] 2 Lloyd's Rep 1

confidence.notes: Findings on each transaction and rejection of both claims are detailed, though corporate structure evidence was incomplete.

notes: Lindsay J held High Court may appoint itself special examiner in Cuba under CPR 34.13 for copyright trial witnesses.

enrichment.short_title: Peer International v Termidor: overseas witness examination in Cuba
key_facts: Peer International and related claimants sued Termidor and Editora Musical de Cuba over ownership of Cuban musical compositions from the 1930s and 1940s.
Video-link evidence from Cuban witnesses failed because of poor quality and frequent breakdowns during the trial.
EMC applied for the judge to examine witnesses in Cuba; claimants opposed on jurisdiction and proposed the Bahamas or Caribbean alternatives.
Cuba is a non-Regulation State where special examination before an appointed examiner is permitted with government consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Mid-trial application on jurisdiction and discretion to take oral evidence overseas during a Chancery copyright trial.
enrichment.outcome: Court held jurisdiction under CPR 34.13(4) to appoint itself special examiner in Cuba subject to Cuban government consent; discretion exercised in favour of Cuba over British Territories.
enrichment.ratio: Examination by a judge appointed as special examiner under CPR 34.13(4) is not a sitting of the High Court outside England and Wales and so is not barred by section 71; where foreign consent is likely, the Letter of Request procedure is unnecessary and Cuba was the expedient venue given witness age, cost and video-link failure.
legal_issues: Whether the High Court has jurisdiction to order overseas examination where a party objects
Whether section 71 SCA 1981 prohibits examination in Cuba
When CPR 34.13(4) applies instead of the Letter of Request procedure
Discretionary choice between Cuba and nearby British Territories as examination venue
linked_authorities: Panayiotou v Sony Music Entertainment (UK) Ltd [1994] Ch 142
St Edmundsbury & Ipswich Diocesan Board of Finance v Clark [197] Ch 323

confidence.notes: Jurisdiction and discretion rulings are fully reasoned with clear procedural machinery.

notes: Beatson J applied Dari and Tum fraud exception to refuse Turkish ECAA entry clearance after passport deception.

enrichment.short_title: Yilmaz v SSHD: fraud bar to Turkish Association Agreement entry
key_facts: Mr Yilmaz, a Turkish national, applied in March 2004 for leave to enter as a self-employed person under the EC-Turkey Association Agreement.
In October 1999 he attempted entry as a returning resident using tampered passport stamps and was granted temporary admission subject to reporting back, which he failed to do.
The Secretary of State refused the application for lack of entry clearance and because of deception in 1999.
The claimant ran a café in Margate in partnership with a settled Turkish national.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of refusal of leave to enter under the Turkish EC Association Agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; fraudulent attempt to gain entry and subsequent breach of temporary admission conditions barred reliance on the Association Agreement.
enrichment.ratio: Following Dari and Tum and Kondova, the fraud exception to the standstill clause applies where a person sought access by fraudulent means even if entry was not ultimately obtained; breach of conditions of temporary admission also renders a person an illegal entrant unable to benefit from the Agreement.
legal_issues: Scope of the fraud exception in R (Dari and Tum) v SSHD
Whether unsuccessful passport deception falls within Kondova
Effect of absconding after temporary admission on ECAA rights
Relevance of pending ECJ reference in Dari and Tum
linked_authorities: R (Dari and Tum) v SSHD [2004] EWCA Civ 788
Kondova v SSHD (Case C-235/99)
Panayotova v Minister voor Vreemdelingenzaken en Integratie (Case C-327/02)

confidence.notes: Fraud exception analysis and alternative illegal-residence ground are clearly articulated.

notes: Divisional Court held prosecution need not prove intoximeter approval where driver elected blood test under section 8(2).

enrichment.short_title: Wright v DPP: breath device approval and section 8(2) blood specimen
key_facts: Mr Wright was stopped driving in Milton Keynes; roadside and station breath tests indicated excess alcohol.
Breath readings of 45 and 43 micrograms led him to elect a blood specimen under section 8(2), which showed 94 mg per 100 ml.
He contended the EC/IR intoximeter was no longer a Secretary of State approved device due to post-approval modifications.
The Crown Court refused to admit evidence on device approval and upheld conviction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Aylesbury Crown Court on admissibility of evidence challenging breath device approval.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; evidence that the device was unapproved was irrelevant where conviction rested on a lawfully elected blood specimen.
enrichment.ratio: Where a driver exercises the section 8(2) option after low breath readings, the prosecution need not prove the intoximeter was of an approved type or working properly; Prince v DPP and Branagan v DPP preclude a meritless technical defence based on device approval.
legal_issues: Whether device type approval must be proved when conviction is based on a section 8(2) blood sample
Effect of post-approval modifications to an approved intoximeter
Whether a lawful breath requirement precludes arguing the device was unapproved
Application of Fox v Chief Constable of Gwent and Howard v Hallett
linked_authorities: Prince v DPP [1996] CLR 343
Branagan v DPP [2000] RTR 235
Fox v Chief Constable of Gwent [1986] 1 AC 281

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme, Crown Court findings and binding authority application are explicit.

notes: Lloyd J on jurisdiction under Brussels Regulation and German law for CVA supervisor's Vehicle 48 claim.

enrichment.short_title: Oakley v UVDL: jurisdiction and choice of law over luxury motorhome
key_facts: Vehicle 48, a Super Nova 1000S motorhome worth hundreds of thousands of pounds, was subject to a March 2003 security transfer from UVDL to German company Behlke.
CVA supervisor Mr Oakley claimed the vehicle belonged to UMIL and sought directions on ownership and Behlke's security interest.
UMIL and UVDL entered liquidation in July 2003 after a failed CVA and asset transfer.
Behlke disputed English jurisdiction and argued German law governed the 2003 contract by oral agreement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issues on jurisdiction and applicable law in supervisor's section 7(4)(a) application.
enrichment.outcome: English jurisdiction upheld under Brussels Regulation Article 6.1 by joinder of UK-domiciled UVDL; 2003 contract governed by German law by oral choice-of-law agreement.
enrichment.ratio: A CVA supervisor's asset claim against a third party is not within the Insolvency Regulation's main proceedings jurisdiction but may be brought in England against a co-defendant domiciled here under Article 6; an oral agreement selecting German law is effective under the Rome Convention where unchallenged at the preliminary issues hearing.
legal_issues: Whether the Insolvency Proceedings Regulation 1346/2000 confers jurisdiction
Application of Brussels Regulation Articles 2, 6 and 23 to Behlke
Whether the 2003 security contract is governed by English or German law
Effect of supervisor proceeding without the liquidator as a party
linked_authorities: Re NT Gallagher & Sons Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 404
Gourdain v Nadler [1979] ECR 733

confidence.notes: Preliminary rulings are clear though ultimate ownership issues remain for trial.

notes: Court of Appeal on section 106 planning obligation deposit; repudiation claim failed but works scope narrowed.

enrichment.short_title: Patel v Brent: section 106 highway payment and delay damages
key_facts: Swaminarayan Hindu Mission trustees deposited £550,000 with Brent LBC under a section 106 agreement for highway improvements at Neasden Lane North/Quainton Street.
Fairclough completed the housing development in 1994 but the council did not commence the Clause 5 works until after proceedings were threatened in 2000.
Trustees sought return of the deposit plus interest for repudiation accepted in August 1999, or alternatively restriction of draw-downs and damages for delay.
The council eventually carried out works including signalisation affecting Braemar Avenue junction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Hart J on construction and enforcement of a section 106 planning obligation.
enrichment.outcome: Repudiation claim rejected; statutory modification/discharge procedure exclusive; appeal allowed on scope of permissible draw-down with inquiry as to Braemar Avenue works; delay damages upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A section 106 deposit creating a trust over money for specified highway works is an extant planning obligation modifiable only under sections 106A–106B, not by contractual repudiation; works must fall within the clause's description as alterations to the Quainton Street junction, not merely engineering best practice extending to a separate junction.
legal_issues: Whether delay amounted to repudiation permitting return of the deposited sum
Exclusive effect of sections 106A and 106B on discharge of planning obligations
Construction of Clause 5.1 highway improvements payment
Whether Braemar Avenue signalisation was within the permitted draw-down

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme and repudiation analysis are clear; quantum of non-qualifying works remitted to inquiry.

notes: Sedley LJ dismissed Part 2 extradition appeals; no entrapment or disclosure duty in US drug sting case.

enrichment.short_title: Jenkins and Benbow v USA: Part 2 extradition and entrapment
key_facts: Benbow and Jenkins were arrested in London in April 2004 after a DEA undercover operation involving proposed trade in radioactive material and large quantities of cocaine.
The United States sought extradition under Part 2 of the Extradition Act 2003 following requests received after 31 December 2003.
Appellants argued entrapment, inadequate disclosure of covert recordings, and parallel extradition schemes violating legal certainty.
Senior District Judge Workman sent the cases to the Home Secretary; entrapment is a substantive defence in US federal law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 103 against district judge's decision to send drug trafficking extradition cases to the Home Secretary.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; no entrapment on the facts, no court power to order disclosure in Part 2 proceedings, and no parallel-scheme uncertainty.
enrichment.ratio: Under Part 2 the requesting state chooses supporting material and the extradition court has no general disclosure power; entrapment is justiciable only if made out on known facts, and offering drugs as payment in an existing covert trade did not incite offenders with no predisposition to drug dealing.
legal_issues: Whether entrapment bars extradition under section 87 and Looseley principles
Whether the court could require US disclosure of DEA recordings
Whether entrapment is solely for the trial court in the requesting state
Whether surviving 1976 and 2003 extradition orders create legal uncertainty
linked_authorities: R v Looseley [2001] UKHL 53
Teixeira de Castro v Portugal (1998) 28 EHRR 101
Serbeh v Governor of HMP Brixton [2002] EWHC 2356 Admin

confidence.notes: Part 2 framework, entrapment analysis and disclosure limits are comprehensively addressed.
